rationale: ASGS Edition 3 publishes the classification, the ARIA+ basis, the five classes and the code structure, and the same classification underlies the 2016 occurrence under the earlier edition.
evidence_quote: Remoteness Areas are identifiable by a 2 digit hierarchical code, comprising the 1-digit State and Territory, and a Remoteness Area identifier.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Remoteness area' with the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation, and gave no warning that the 2016 and 2021 codings rest on different ASGS editions.

value_domain: ASCRG religious affiliation code
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2021, Religious affiliation (RELP)
variable_description: The religion a person reported, coded to the Australian Standard Classification of Religious Groups. ABS states that the variable "records a person's religious affiliation" and that "answering this Census question is optional", which makes it the one substantive Census item a person may lawfully leave blank. The classification is hierarchical, with 151 detailed groups nesting into 38 narrow and 10 broad groups, and 'No religion' is a coded response in its own right rather than a missing value.
value_definition: A hierarchical ASCRG 2016 code: one digit for the broad group, two or three digits for the narrow group and four digits for the detailed religious group, giving 151 categories at the finest level. 'Not stated' and 'No religion' are separate codes.
limitation: It records affiliation as stated, not belief, practice or attendance, so a detailed denomination code does not mean the person takes part. Because the question is voluntary, 'not stated' — 6.9 per cent in 2021, down from 9.1 per cent in 2016 — is not missing at random — it mixes refusal with people who simply skipped an optional box. 'No religion' and 'not stated' are different codes and pooling them will overstate secularity.
rationale: The Census Dictionary page for this mnemonic gives the definition, names ASCRG 2016 as the classification, sets out the four hierarchical levels and their category counts, and states that the question is optional.
evidence_quote: This variable records a person's religious affiliation. Answering this Census question is optional.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried only 'Religious Affiliation' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not name ASCRG, did not warn that the question is voluntary, and did not distinguish 'No religion' from 'Not stated'.

value_domain: Census couple relationship category
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2021, Relationship as reported for couples (RLCP)
variable_description: How a person in a coresident couple described their partner — as a husband, wife or partner, or as a de facto partner — crossed with whether the couple is opposite-sex or same-sex. ABS defines it as recording "the partner relationship as it is reported for all couples in an occupied dwelling", so the categories are labelled 'as reported' and follow the wording the couple used on the form. It sits on the person record, so both members of a couple carry a value, and SSCF on the family record summarises the same information one level up. Everyone not living with a partner is not applicable.
value_definition: Four substantive categories crossing husband, wife or partner as reported against de facto partner as reported, each split by opposite-sex and same-sex couple, plus @ for not applicable and V for overseas visitor.
limitation: It describes the couple the person lives with, not legal marital status: someone legally married but living apart from their spouse is not applicable here while MSTP still records them as married. The registered against de facto split is also a reporting distinction, taken from how the couple described themselves on the form rather than checked against any marriage register.
rationale: The Census Dictionary page defines this mnemonic, sets out the four couple categories and the supplementary codes, and states that it is derived from the relationship in household and sex questions.
evidence_quote: This variable records the partner relationship as it is reported for all couples in an occupied dwelling.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Relationship as Reported for Couples' with the generic no-value-list sentence as definition and limitation, so it did not say that this is the reported rather than the legal relationship, or how it relates to RLHP and MSTP.

value_domain: Census household relationship code (grandchildren variant)
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2021, Relationship in household (including grandchildren) (RLGP)
variable_description: The person's relationship to their family reference person, coded on the variant of the scale that keeps grandchildren visible. It carries the same ABS definition as RLHP — it "describes the relationship of each person in a family to the family reference person" — but adds a dependent student grandchild category and codes a lone grandparent with no parent-child relationship as a lone parent rather than as a grandparent. ABS restricts it to use with the grandparent variables CTGP and FMGF, which sit beside it, rather than with the standard family composition variables. Reach for RLHP for ordinary household work and RLGP only when grandchildren are the point.
value_definition: Thirty-one categories: couple and lone parent roles; children under 15, dependent students and non-dependent children each split by natural or adopted, step, foster and grandchild; other relatives; non-family members; and non-classifiable codes, plus @ for not applicable.
limitation: It is not interchangeable with RLHP and must not be crossed with the standard family composition variables, because its lone parent and grandchild rules differ and the two will disagree on the same household. Like RLHP it describes coresidence at one moment, so a grandchild code means the child was living there on Census night, not that the grandparent has care or guardianship of them.
rationale: The Census Dictionary page for this mnemonic names the two ways it departs from RLHP, lists the 31 categories and states which companion variables it may be used with.
evidence_quote: This variable describes the relationship of each person in a family to the family reference person.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried only 'Relationship in Household (including grandchildren)' with the generic no-value-list sentence printed twice, so it did not explain why a second relationship variable exists or that ABS restricts what it can be crossed with.

value_domain: Census household relationship code
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2021, Relationship in household (RLHP)
variable_description: Each person's position in their household, expressed as their relationship to the family or household reference person. ABS defines it as describing "the relationship of each person in a family to the family reference person", and adds that "where a person is not part of a family, that person's relationship to the household reference person is captured". It is derived during processing from the relationship-to-Person-1 answers together with sex, age and student status, and it is the variable that lets person records be aggregated into the family and dwelling tables. RPIP on the same row marks who the reference person is.
value_definition: Thirty-four categories grouped as husband, wife or partner; lone parent; child under 15; dependent student; non-dependent child; other related individual; non-family member; and non-classifiable, plus supplementary codes for visitors and not applicable.
limitation: It is measured against the reference person only, so two people both coded 'other related individual' tell you nothing about how they are related to each other, and no full relationship matrix can be rebuilt from it. It also cannot be trusted for step-parenthood in 2021: ABS identified an overcount of step children, with a matching undercount of natural or adopted children, in couple families with a temporarily absent spouse in several states and territories.
rationale: The Census Dictionary page defines the mnemonic, describes how the variable is derived from several form questions, lists the category groups and publishes the 2021 step child overcount as a data quality issue.
evidence_quote: This variable describes the relationship of each person in a family to the family reference person. Where a person is not part of a family, that person's relationship to the household reference person is captured.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Relationship in Household' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation, so it did not say the coding is relative to a reference person, nor flag the 2021 step child overcount.

value_domain: Residential status in a non-private dwelling
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2021, Residential status in a non-private dwelling (RLNP)
variable_description: For a person counted in a non-private dwelling, whether they were there as staff or as someone being accommodated. ABS defines it as describing "the residential status of each person in a non-private dwelling", and it applies to everyone in such a dwelling on Census night. NPDD on the dwelling record says what kind of establishment it was — a hospital, a prison, a hostel, a hotel — and RLNP says which side of it the person was on. Everyone in an occupied private dwelling is not applicable.
value_definition: Two substantive output categories, 'owner, proprietor, staff and family' and 'guest, patient, inmate, other resident', plus supplementary codes for not stated, not applicable and overseas visitor. Not applicable covers people in occupied private dwellings and in migratory, off-shore and shipping areas.
limitation: The resident category pools situations with nothing in common — a prisoner, a hospital patient, an aged care resident and a hotel guest all take the same code — so it cannot count institutionalised people without joining to NPDD on the dwelling. It also says nothing about how long the person had been there or whether they usually live there.
rationale: The Census Dictionary page defines this mnemonic, gives its two output categories, states who it applies to and what falls into not applicable.
evidence_quote: This variable describes the residential status of each person in a non-private dwelling.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried only 'Residential Status in a Non-Private Dwelling' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not say the choice is staff against resident, nor that NPDD is needed to tell a prison from a hotel.

value_domain: Weekly rent in whole dollars
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2021, Rent (weekly) dollar values (RNTD)
variable_description: The exact weekly rent reported for this dwelling, in whole dollars. ABS defines it as recording "the individual dollar amounts of rent paid by households on a weekly basis for the dwelling in which they were counted on Census Night", so it is a dwelling-level amount attached to the household that was there. It is the input to RNTRD, which bands the same figure, and to RAID, which compares it with imputed household income. Only rented occupied private dwellings carry a value.
value_definition: A four-digit whole-dollar amount, codes 0001 to 9999 standing for $1 to $9,999 per week, with &&&& for not stated and @@@@ for not applicable.
limitation: It is rent for the whole dwelling, not per person, so a five-bedroom share house looks expensive beside a couple's flat and no per-head figure can be taken from it without dividing by the household count. Owners are never zero: not applicable covers dwellings owned outright, owned with a mortgage, under shared equity or life tenure schemes, occupied rent free, unoccupied dwellings and non-private dwellings, so a missing value is not evidence of free housing.
rationale: The Census Dictionary page defines the mnemonic, gives the code range and the supplementary codes, and lists exactly which tenure types fall into not applicable.
evidence_quote: This variable records the individual dollar amounts of rent paid by households on a weekly basis for the dwelling in which they were counted on Census Night.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Rent (weekly) Dollar Values' with the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation, so it gave neither the dollar range nor the point that not applicable and zero rent are different things.

value_domain: Weekly rent range
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2021, Rent (weekly) ranges (RNTRD)
variable_description: The dwelling's weekly rent grouped into bands rather than exact dollars. ABS defines it as recording "the rent paid for a dwelling on a weekly basis in ranges", and it is derived directly from RNTD, which sits beside it on the same dwelling record. It exists because standard Census products such as QuickStats and Community Profiles publish rent in bands; where RNTD is available, use that instead. The bands run from $1 to $74 up to $950 and over.
value_definition: Twenty-five ordered ranges, coded 01 for $1 to $74 through to 25 for $950 and over, plus not stated and not applicable.
limitation: The top band is open-ended, so a mean rent built from band midpoints understates rents in expensive markets and will not match a mean built from RNTD. The band edges are nominal dollars set for the Census they belong to, so rents drift up the bands through inflation alone and a band share should not be compared across Census years without first checking that the ranges match.
rationale: The Census Dictionary page defines the mnemonic, states that it is derived from RNTD, gives the number of bands and their end points, and names the products it is published in.
evidence_quote: This variable records the rent paid for a dwelling on a weekly basis in ranges.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried only 'Rent (weekly) Ranges' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not say the bands come straight from RNTD or that the top band is open-ended.

value_domain: Family or household reference person indicator
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2021, Family/household reference person indicator (RPIP)
variable_description: Marks which household member is the reference person that everyone else's relationship is coded against, and which family within the household they anchor. ABS defines it as a variable that "identifies a household member as the reference person used in Census coding", with separate codes for the first, second and third family in a multi-family household. The reference person must be a usual resident aged 15 or over who was present on Census night, and is normally Person 1 on the form unless another person suits better. It is the key that makes RLHP and RLGP interpretable.
value_definition: Five substantive codes: reference person in the primary family (1), second family (2) and third family (3), reference person in a non-family household (4) and other household member (5), plus @ for not applicable and V for overseas visitor.
limitation: It is a processing device, not a status. ABS states the designation does not mean the person is the head of the household, so it must not stand in for the main earner, the owner or the decision maker. Selecting on code 1 also returns one person per family rather than one per dwelling, so a household holding two or three families will be counted more than once.
rationale: The Census Dictionary page defines the mnemonic, lists the seven codes, sets out the selection criteria and states explicitly that the designation is not a head-of-household marker.
evidence_quote: This variable identifies a household member as the reference person used in Census coding.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Family/Household Reference Person Indicator' with the generic no-value-list sentence as definition and limitation, so it never warned against reading the reference person as the household head or explained the multi-family codes.

value_domain: ASGS Statistical Area Level 1 code (usual residence one year ago)
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2021, Place of usual residence one year ago (PUR1P)
variable_description: The SA1 the person usually lived in one year before the Census, which is how twelve-month internal migration is measured on the person record. ABS defines the underlying variable as recording "the geographic area in which a person usually lived one year before the Census", answered from a form question naming the date a year earlier. Comparing it with SA1UCP on the same row shows whether the person moved and between which areas, and UAI1P states the move directly. Children aged under one year are not applicable.
value_definition: An eleven-digit ASGS SA1 code: one digit for state, two for SA4, two for SA3, four for SA2 and two for the SA1 within its SA2. SA1s hold 200 to 800 people, about 400 on average.
limitation: The address is self-reported a year after the fact, so a vaguely written answer is coded no finer than a capital city or a state and never reaches an SA1 at all; ABS publishes the variable at SA2 as its base output level for that reason. Non-response was 6.0 per cent in 2021 and 8.6 per cent in 2016. A code that changes between Censuses can also be a boundary change rather than a move, because SA1 boundaries are redrawn each Census.
rationale: The Census Dictionary page for place of usual residence one year ago defines what the address refers to, lists the special codes and gives the non-response rates; the SA1 geography and its code structure come from the ASGS. Confidence is medium because ABS publishes this question at SA2 base level, while the PLIDA column carries it at SA1.
evidence_quote: This variable records the geographic area in which a person usually lived one year before the Census.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried only 'SA1 of usual residence - one year ago' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not say the address is self-reported, that non-response is around 6 per cent, or that SA1 boundaries move between Censuses.

value_domain: ASGS Statistical Area Level 1 code (usual residence five years ago)
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2021, Place of usual residence five years ago (PUR5P)
variable_description: The SA1 the person usually lived in five years before the Census, which lines a person up against the previous Census night. ABS defines the underlying variable as recording "the geographic area in which a person usually lived five years before the Census", so with SA1UCP on the same row it gives a five-year migration flow, and with SA1U1P it separates a recent move from an older one. UAI5P on the same record states whether the address changed at all. Children aged under five years are not applicable.
value_definition: An eleven-digit ASGS SA1 code (state, SA4, SA3, SA2, SA1), with supplementary categories for capital city not further defined, state or territory not further defined, migratory-offshore-shipping, no usual address, overseas and not stated.
limitation: Five-year recall is weaker than one-year recall and non-response is higher, at 6.9 per cent in 2021 and 8.0 per cent in 2016, so a missing value here is common and not random. It records only the two end points: a person who moved three times and came back looks as though they never left.
rationale: The Census Dictionary page for place of usual residence five years ago gives the definition, the base output level and the non-response rates; the SA1 code structure comes from the ASGS. Confidence is medium because ABS outputs the question at SA2 while this PLIDA column carries SA1.
evidence_quote: This variable records the geographic area in which a person usually lived five years before the Census.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'SA1 of usual residence - five years ago' with the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation, so it did not give the non-response rate or say that intermediate moves are invisible.

value_domain: ASGS Statistical Area Level 1 code (dwelling location)
value_source: ABS Census geography glossary, Statistical Area Level 1 (SA1)
variable_description: The SA1 the dwelling itself sits in, on the dwelling record for all three Census years and on the 2021 family record. ABS describes SA1s as areas "designed to maximise the geographic detail available for Census of Population and Housing data while maintaining confidentiality", built from whole mesh blocks and holding 200 to 800 people. It is the finest geography on the 2011 and 2016 dwelling records; the 2021 dwelling record also carries the mesh block, MBUCD. SA2UCD, SA3UCD and SA4UCD beside it are the same location rolled up. Unlike the person-level SA1UCP it describes where the dwelling is, so unoccupied dwellings carry it too.
value_definition: An eleven-digit fully hierarchical ASGS code — state, SA4, SA3, SA2, SA1 — with 61,845 SA1s in Edition 3 including 34 non-spatial special purpose codes.
limitation: An SA1 is a confidentiality unit, not a neighbourhood or a suburb, and its boundaries are redrawn at every Census, so the 2011, 2016 and 2021 dwelling tables cannot be joined on this code without a correspondence file. For 2011 and 2016 it is also as fine as the release goes, and street address is never available, so two dwellings sharing an SA1 may be a kilometre apart.
rationale: The Census geography glossary gives the Census-specific definition of SA1 and the ASGS Edition 3 page gives the code structure, the count and the population range.
evidence_quote: Statistical Areas Level 1 (SA1s) are designed to maximise the geographic detail available for Census of Population and Housing data while maintaining confidentiality.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried only 'SA1 of dwelling address' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not give the code structure or warn that SA1 boundaries change between Census years.

value_domain: ASGS Statistical Area Level 1 code (usual residence)
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2021, Place of usual residence (PURP)
variable_description: The SA1 where the person usually lived, the finest geography on the 2011 and 2016 person records and one level above the 2021 mesh block column MBUCP. ABS defines place of usual residence as "the geographic area in which a person usually lives" and notes that "it may or may not be the place where the person was counted on Census Night", so this can differ from the dwelling's SA1UCD for anyone away from home. Usual residence means the address at which a person lives or intends to live for six months or more. Where the reported address was incomplete the value is imputed, and IFPURP on the same person record flags that.
value_definition: An eleven-digit ASGS SA1 code (state, SA4, SA3, SA2, SA1), coded up from the mesh block the address falls in. SA1s hold 200 to 800 people.
limitation: Non-response at SA1 level was 4.4 per cent in 2021 and 5.5 per cent in 2016, and imputation fills part of that, so an SA1 code is not always a reported address — read IFPURP before treating it as one. Sharing an SA1 is not living together: an SA1 holds a few hundred people, so this column cannot be used to identify a household. The six-month rule is also self-applied, and respondents often give the address they think of as home rather than one that meets the test.
rationale: The Census Dictionary page for place of usual residence defines the concept, states the six-month rule, describes the imputation and gives the SA1-level non-response rates for 2016 and 2021.
evidence_quote: This variable records the geographic area in which a person usually lives. It may or may not be the place where the person was counted on Census Night.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'SA1 of usual address' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not distinguish usual residence from place of enumeration or mention that some values are imputed.

value_domain: ASGS Statistical Area Level 2 code (usual residence one year ago)
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2021, Place of usual residence one year ago (PUR1P)
variable_description: The SA2 the person usually lived in a year before the Census, and the level at which ABS actually publishes the one-year-ago question. The dictionary states that the base area output for this variable is Statistical Area Level 2, and that "for people whose place of usual residence one year ago was the same as their place of usual residence on Census Night, PUR1P is automatically derived from Place of usual residence (PURP)". Paired with SA2UCP on the same row it gives a twelve-month migration flow between SA2s. Children under one year old are not applicable.
value_definition: A nine-digit ASGS SA2 code (state, SA4, SA3, SA2), covering about 2,470 areas, with special categories for capital city not further defined, state or territory not further defined, migratory-offshore-shipping, no usual address, overseas and not stated.
limitation: It cannot see a move within an SA2, which is where a large share of moves happen, so an unchanged code is not evidence the person stayed at the same address. 'Overseas' is a single code with no country attached, so it marks an arrival without saying from where and does not separate a returning Australian from a new migrant. Non-response was 6.0 per cent in 2021 and 8.6 per cent in 2016.
rationale: The Census Dictionary page for the one-year-ago question names SA2 as the base output level, explains the automatic derivation for non-movers, lists the special codes and gives the non-response rates.
evidence_quote: For people whose place of usual residence one year ago was the same as their place of usual residence on Census Night, PUR1P is automatically derived from Place of usual residence (PURP).
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'SA2 of usual address 1 year ago' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not say that non-movers are filled from the current address rather than reported afresh.

value_domain: ASGS Statistical Area Level 2 code (usual residence five years ago)
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2021, Place of usual residence five years ago (PUR5P)
variable_description: The SA2 the person usually lived in five years before the Census, the standard basis for ABS internal migration tables. ABS defines the source variable as recording "the geographic area in which a person usually lived five years before the Census", with SA2 as the base output area that higher ASGS levels are aggregated from. Read against SA2UCP it gives a five-year origin-destination flow, and against SA2U1P it separates a move in the last year from an earlier one. Children under five are not applicable.
value_definition: A nine-digit ASGS SA2 code (state, SA4, SA3, SA2), with supplementary categories for capital city not further defined, state or territory not further defined, migratory-offshore-shipping, no usual address, overseas and not stated.
limitation: It gives two snapshots five years apart and nothing between, so return migration and repeated moves cancel out and the count of movers is a floor, not a total. Non-response was 6.9 per cent in 2021 and 8.0 per cent in 2016, higher than for the one-year question, which biases migration rates downward if 'not stated' is dropped. SA2 boundaries also change between ASGS editions, so the origin and destination codes are not always on the same map.
rationale: The Census Dictionary page for the five-year-ago question gives the definition, names SA2 as the base output level and publishes the 2016 and 2021 non-response rates.
evidence_quote: This variable records the geographic area in which a person usually lived five years before the Census.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'SA2 of usual address 5 years ago' with the generic no-value-list sentence as definition and limitation, so it did not flag the higher non-response or that intermediate moves are lost.

value_domain: ASGS Statistical Area Level 2 code (dwelling location)
value_source: ABS Census geography glossary, Statistical Area Level 2 (SA2)
variable_description: The SA2 containing the dwelling, and the level most Census dwelling analysis is done at. ABS describes SA2s as "medium-sized general purpose areas built up from whole Statistical Areas Level 1 (SA1s)", designed to represent communities that interact socially and economically. Because SA2 is the smallest area for which many non-Census ABS statistics are published, it is the usual join key from a Census dwelling to external regional data. It also appears on the 2021 family record, where it means the SA2 of the dwelling the family was counted in.
value_definition: A nine-digit hierarchical ASGS code built from the SA1 code without its last two digits — state, SA4, SA3, SA2 — with about 2,470 SA2s in Edition 3.
limitation: SA2 boundaries are rebuilt between ASGS editions, so identical digits in the 2016 and 2021 dwelling tables do not guarantee the same area and the years should be linked through a correspondence file. An SA2 is also designed around community of interest, not service delivery, so it does not nest inside a local government area, a state electoral division or a health district.
rationale: The Census geography glossary gives the Census-specific SA2 definition, and the ASGS Edition 3 main structure pages give the count and the hierarchical code.
evidence_quote: Statistical Areas Level 2 (SA2s) are medium-sized general purpose areas built up from whole Statistical Areas Level 1 (SA1s).
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried only 'SA2 of dwelling address' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not explain why SA2 is the practical level for joining Census dwellings to other ABS data.

value_domain: ASGS Statistical Area Level 2 code (usual residence)
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2021, Place of usual residence (PURP)
variable_description: The SA2 where the person usually lived, the level most place-of-usual-residence output is published at. It is the coarser twin of SA1UCP on the same row, and the safer choice where SA1 counts would be too small to use. ABS notes that usual residence "may or may not be the place where the person was counted on Census Night", so a person enumerated interstate is still placed at home here. Non-response at SA2 level was 4.3 per cent in 2021, and IFPURP flags values that were imputed from an incomplete address.
value_definition: A nine-digit ASGS SA2 code (state, SA4, SA3, SA2), coded up from the mesh block of the reported address, with about 2,470 areas covering Australia.
limitation: It cannot support any claim about who a person lives with or near: an SA2 holds thousands of people, and no dwelling-level inference follows from a shared code. Comparing this column with SA2U1P or SA2U5P also gives a move between areas, not a distance, since an SA2 pair says nothing about how far apart the two addresses were.
rationale: The Census Dictionary page for place of usual residence defines the concept, describes the imputation and gives the SA2-level non-response rate; the SA2 code structure comes from the ASGS.
evidence_quote: This variable records the geographic area in which a person usually lives. It may or may not be the place where the person was counted on Census Night.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'SA2 of usual address' with the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation, so it did not distinguish usual residence from place of enumeration or mention imputation.

value_domain: ASGS Statistical Area Level 2 code (workplace address)
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2021, Place of work (POWP)
variable_description: The SA2 containing the address where the person worked in the week before the Census, on the 2011 person record. It is the SA2 rollup of place of work, which ABS defines as recording "the geographic area in which a person worked in the week before Census Night" and which "is determined from written responses to the Business name and Workplace address questions on the Census form", coded at its finest level to a destination zone. STEWKADP beside it is the same workplace at state level, and comparing either with SA2UCP or STEUCP gives a commute between home and work. The registry's own description for this column is truncated to 'SA', so the mnemonic is the guide: SA2, work address, person.
value_definition: A nine-digit ASGS SA2 code (state, SA4, SA3, SA2), aggregated up from the destination zone the workplace address was coded to. Employed people aged 15 and over are in scope; everyone else takes a not applicable code.
limitation: It records one workplace for the reference week, so a person with two jobs or several work sites appears at a single place and the rest are uncounted. It is also not a commuting distance: a home and work SA2 pair gives the ends of a journey, not its length or route. ABS also instructs a person with no fixed place of work to give a depot address, or nothing at all where there is no depot, so for them the SA2 is not where any work was done.
rationale: The Census Dictionary place-of-work page states how the workplace address is captured and coded and who is in scope; the SA2 geography and code structure come from the ASGS. Confidence is medium because the registry's description for this column is truncated and the reading rests on the mnemonic and on the neighbouring STEWKADP column.
evidence_quote: This variable records the geographic area in which a person worked in the week before Census Night.
supersedes_rationale: The entry's description was the two-letter fragment 'SA', with the generic no-value-list sentence printed twice, so the page said nothing at all about what the column holds.

value_domain: ASGS Statistical Area Level 3 code (dwelling location)
value_source: ABS Census geography glossary, Statistical Area Level 3 (SA3)
variable_description: The SA3 region containing the dwelling, one step coarser than SA2UCD on the same record. ABS describes SA3s as areas that "provide a standardised regional breakup of Australia", built from whole SA2s and sized to represent regional service catchments and urban districts. On the Census dwelling table it is the level at which dwelling characteristics such as tenure, rent and bedroom counts can be compared between regions without small-count suppression. There are about 359 SA3s covering the country.
value_definition: A five-digit hierarchical ASGS code — one digit for state, two for SA4, two for SA3 — obtained by truncating the SA1 or SA2 code on the same row.
limitation: An SA3 is a statistical region, not an administrative one, so it does not line up with a local government area or a state electoral division and cannot be used to attribute a dwelling to a council. Its boundaries also change between ASGS editions, so an SA3 with the same code in 2016 and 2021 need not cover the same ground.
rationale: The Census geography glossary defines SA3 for Census use, and the ASGS Edition 3 structure gives the region count and the hierarchical code that SA1 truncates to.
evidence_quote: Statistical Areas Level 3 (SA3s) provide a standardised regional breakup of Australia.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'SA3 of dwelling address' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence, so it did not say what an SA3 is for or that it is derived by truncating the finer code.

value_domain: ASGS Statistical Area Level 3 code (usual residence)
value_source: ABS Census geography glossary, Statistical Area Level 3 (SA3)
variable_description: The SA3 region the person usually lived in, on the person record for all three Census years. ABS describes SA3s as areas that "provide a standardised regional breakup of Australia", each built from whole SA2s, which makes this the level most regional analysis of Census person data is done at. It is the same address as SA1UCP and SA2UCP beside it, coded coarser, so counts stay publishable where finer geography would be suppressed. Because it is usual residence, a person counted away from home is placed where they live.
value_definition: A five-digit hierarchical ASGS code (state, SA4, SA3), being the first five digits of the person's SA1 code, over about 359 regions.
limitation: SA3s are large and internally varied — a single SA3 can hold both an established inner suburb and a new estate — so an SA3 average hides most of the difference between the people in it. It is also not a labour market, a health district or a school catchment, so it cannot be used to attach a person to a service area.
rationale: The Census geography glossary gives the Census-specific SA3 definition and the ASGS Edition 3 structure gives the count and the hierarchical code relationship to SA1.
evidence_quote: Statistical Areas Level 3 (SA3s) provide a standardised regional breakup of Australia.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'SA3 of usual address' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not say why an SA3 exists or what is lost by using it instead of SA2.

value_domain: ASGS Statistical Area Level 4 code (dwelling location)
value_source: ABS Census geography glossary, Statistical Area Level 4 (SA4)
variable_description: The SA4 containing the dwelling, the coarsest sub-state geography on the Census dwelling record. ABS describes SA4s as areas that "provide the best sub-state socio-economic breakdown in the ASGS", and they are sized to carry Labour Force Survey estimates, which makes SA4 the level at which Census dwelling results line up with monthly labour force data. There are 108 SA4s covering Australia. It is the same dwelling as SA1UCD, SA2UCD and SA3UCD, coded at its broadest.
value_definition: A three-digit hierarchical ASGS code — one digit for state or territory, two for the SA4 — being the first three digits of the SA1 code on the same row.
limitation: An SA4 is far too coarse to describe a housing market: one SA4 can hold an inner-city apartment belt and an outer suburban fringe together, so a dwelling attribute averaged here hides nearly all of its variation. Despite being built for labour force estimation it is not a labour market area in its own right, and commuting crosses SA4 boundaries routinely.
rationale: The Census geography glossary defines SA4 for Census use, and the ASGS Edition 3 structure gives the count and the hierarchical code that the finer codes truncate to.
evidence_quote: Statistical Areas Level 4 (SA4s) provide the best sub-state socio-economic breakdown in the ASGS.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried only 'SA4 of dwelling address' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not say that SA4 is the Labour Force Survey geography or how coarse it is.

value_domain: ASGS Statistical Area Level 4 code (usual residence)
value_source: ABS Census geography glossary, Statistical Area Level 4 (SA4)
variable_description: The SA4 the person usually lived in, the broadest sub-state geography on the Census person record. ABS describes SA4s as the areas that "provide the best sub-state socio-economic breakdown in the ASGS", and because they are designed to support Labour Force Survey estimates this is the level at which Census labour force counts can be read against the monthly survey. About 108 SA4s cover Australia, so a code here identifies a large region such as a group of city suburbs or a whole rural zone. The finer SA3UCP, SA2UCP and SA1UCP on the same row describe the same address.
value_definition: A three-digit hierarchical ASGS code (state or territory, then SA4), being the first three digits of the person's SA1 code.
limitation: The regions are so large that an SA4 rate conceals most within-region variation, and a difference between two SA4s can be driven entirely by their internal composition. Because it is usual residence, it also cannot be used to describe where people were during the day: an SA4 of residence tells you nothing about where its workers travel to.
rationale: The Census geography glossary gives the SA4 definition used for Census output, and the ASGS Edition 3 structure supplies the count and the hierarchical code.
evidence_quote: Statistical Areas Level 4 (SA4s) provide the best sub-state socio-economic breakdown in the ASGS.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'SA4 of usual address' with the generic no-value-list sentence as definition and limitation, so it did not say what an SA4 is designed for or how coarse the resulting regions are.

value_domain: Supported accommodation dwelling flag
value_source: ABS, Understanding the Census and Census Data, Australia 2016, SAFD Supported Accommodation Flag
variable_description: Marks the dwelling as one providing supported accommodation for people without a permanent home, which is how the Census identifies homelessness service settings. ABS describes the flag as applying to "dwellings that provide supported accommodation for persons without a permanent residence", and notes that "this data is available by request only". It was introduced for the 2011 Census, unchanged for 2016, and ABS intends it to be used with NPDD, the type of non-private dwelling, which separates a boarding house from a hostel for the homeless. It appears on the 2011 and 2016 dwelling records only.
value_definition: A flag on the dwelling record separating supported accommodation establishments from all other dwellings, with a not applicable category for dwellings out of scope.
limitation: It flags the dwelling, not the person, so it says where someone was counted rather than whether they were homeless — ABS estimates homelessness from a separate operational definition, and not everyone staying in supported accommodation meets it. It also misses the larger part of the homeless population: people sleeping rough, staying temporarily with others, or in severely crowded dwellings are not in a flagged establishment at all.
rationale: The ABS 2016 Census information page for this exact mnemonic states what the flag covers, when it was introduced and which variable it is meant to be used with. Confidence is medium because ABS restricts the item to request-only release and does not publish the code list.
evidence_quote: dwellings that provide supported accommodation for persons without a permanent residence. This data is available by request only.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried only 'Supported Accommodation Flag' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not say the flag is a dwelling attribute rather than a homelessness measure, or that it pairs with NPDD.

value_domain: ASGS Suburbs and Localities code
value_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, Suburbs and Localities
variable_description: The suburb or locality the dwelling sits in, which is the closest the Census comes to a place name a resident would recognise. ABS defines Suburbs and Localities as "an ABS Mesh Block approximation of the officially recognised boundaries of suburbs (in cities and larger towns) and localities (outside cities and larger towns) as defined by the State and Territory governments of Australia", and warns that these approximations "do not match official legal boundaries and should only be used for statistical purposes". It appears on the 2021 dwelling record and on the 2021 family record, alongside POAD and LGAD, the other named-place approximations. Suburbs and Localities were called State Suburbs before ASGS Edition 3.
value_definition: A five-digit code: one digit for state or territory then a four-digit sequential identifier starting at 0001, covering 15,353 suburbs and localities in ASGS Edition 3.
limitation: The boundary is a mesh block approximation, so a dwelling near the edge of a suburb can be allocated to the neighbouring one, and the code must never be used to decide whether an address legally falls in a suburb. Suburb names also repeat between states, so the state digit is part of the identity and a name on its own is not unique.
rationale: The ASGS Edition 3 page defines the structure, gives the code format and count, and carries the ABS warning that these are approximations of legal boundaries.
evidence_quote: Suburbs and Localities, formerly State Suburbs, are an ABS Mesh Block approximation of the officially recognised boundaries of suburbs (in cities and larger towns) and localities (outside cities and larger towns) as defined by the State and Territory governments of Australia.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried only 'Suburbs and localities (en)' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not say the boundaries are approximations that must not be used for legal purposes.

value_domain: ASGS Suburbs and Localities code (usual residence)
value_source: ABS Census geography glossary, Suburbs and Localities (SAL)
variable_description: The suburb or locality the person usually lived in, on the 2021 person record. ABS describes Suburbs and Localities as "an approximation of the officially recognised boundaries of suburbs (in cities and larger towns) and localities (outside of cities and larger towns)", built from whole mesh blocks. Because this is coded to usual residence, it can name a different suburb from SALD on the dwelling the person was actually counted in. It is the geography most useful for presenting person-level Census results to a general audience, since a suburb name means something an SA1 code does not.
value_definition: A five-digit ASGS code combining a one-digit state or territory identifier with a four-digit suburb or locality identifier, over 15,353 areas in Edition 3.
limitation: Suburbs vary enormously in population, from a few dozen people to tens of thousands, so counts by suburb are not comparable with each other and small suburbs will often be suppressed or perturbed. The approximation is also rebuilt when state gazetted boundaries change, so the same suburb code is not guaranteed to cover the same ground in a later edition.
rationale: The Census geography glossary gives the definition used for Census output, and the ASGS Edition 3 page supplies the code structure and the count.
evidence_quote: Suburbs and Localities (SALs) are an approximation of the officially recognised boundaries of suburbs (in cities and larger towns) and localities (outside of cities and larger towns).
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Suburbs and localities (ur)' with the generic no-value-list sentence as definition and limitation, so it did not say that suburbs differ wildly in size or that this is usual residence rather than where the person was counted.

value_domain: ASGS State Electoral Division code (2022 boundaries)
value_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, State Electoral Divisions
variable_description: The dwelling placed on state electoral division boundaries as they stood in 2022, sitting beside SEDD which places the same dwelling on the 2021 boundaries. ABS defines State Electoral Divisions as "an ABS Mesh Block approximation of state electoral districts as defined by state and territory electoral commissions", and updates that approximation each year that a redistribution occurs — the 2022 update took in the New South Wales and Victorian redistributions. Use this column when reading 2021 Census counts against an election run on post-2021 boundaries. Only the 2021 dwelling record carries it.
value_definition: A five-digit code, one digit for state or territory and four for the division, on the 2022 boundary set; Victoria and Tasmania use a two-part identifier reflecting both lower and upper house regions.
limitation: The dwelling did not move: a difference between SED22D and SEDD is a redistribution, not a relocation, and reading the pair as change over time will invent movement that never happened. Like every SED coding it is a mesh block approximation, so it cannot determine which division a particular address actually votes in.
rationale: The ASGS Edition 3 page defines the structure, gives the code format and states that boundaries are updated annually as redistributions occur, naming the 2022 update. That the '22' in the mnemonic is the boundary vintage follows from the custodian's own description, '2022 boundaries'.
evidence_quote: State Electoral Divisions are an ABS Mesh Block approximation of state electoral districts as defined by state and territory electoral commissions.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried only 'State electoral divisions (2022 boundaries) (en)' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it never explained why two boundary vintages sit on the same record or warned that a difference between them is not a move.

value_domain: ASGS State Electoral Division code (2021 boundaries)
value_source: ABS Census geography glossary, State Electoral Division (SED)
variable_description: The state or territory lower house electorate the dwelling falls in, on the boundaries in force at the 2021 Census. ABS defines a State Electoral Division as "an area legally prescribed for the purpose of returning one or more members to the State or Territory lower houses of parliament", approximated for statistical use from whole mesh blocks. SED22D on the same 2021 dwelling record places the dwelling on the 2022 boundaries instead, and CEDD is the Commonwealth equivalent. It is the column to use when matching Census dwelling counts to the electorate map as it stood on Census night.
value_definition: A five-digit code combining a one-digit state or territory identifier with a four-digit division identifier, over 452 divisions in ASGS Edition 3 including 19 non-spatial special purpose codes.
limitation: It is a mesh block approximation of a legal boundary, so it cannot decide which electorate a given address votes in and must not be used for enrolment or entitlement work. Division names are also reused across redistributions, so a division with the same name is not the same area in different years.
rationale: The Census geography glossary gives the definition used for Census output and the ASGS Edition 3 page supplies the mesh block approximation caveat, the code structure and the division count.
evidence_quote: An SED is an area legally prescribed for the purpose of returning one or more members to the State or Territory lower houses of parliament.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'State electoral divisions (2021 boundaries) (en)' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not say the boundaries are approximations or how the column relates to SED22D.

value_domain: ASGS State Electoral Division code (2021 boundaries, usual residence)
value_source: ABS Census geography glossary, State Electoral Division (SED)
variable_description: The state electorate covering the person's usual address, on the boundaries in force at the 2021 Census. ABS defines a State Electoral Division as "an area legally prescribed for the purpose of returning one or more members to the State or Territory lower houses of parliament". Because this is coded to usual residence rather than to where the person was counted, it places a person where they would be enrolled rather than where they slept on Census night, which is the distinction that matters for electorate profiles. SEDP22 on the same person record gives the 2022 boundary version.
value_definition: A five-digit ASGS code (state or territory, then division) on the 2021 boundary set, over 452 divisions including 19 special purpose codes.
limitation: The Census counts everyone in Australia, including children, non-citizens and adults who are not enrolled, so a headcount by this column is a resident population and will be far larger than the electorate roll. The coding is also a mesh block approximation, so it cannot confirm which division any individual address belongs to.
rationale: The Census geography glossary defines SED for Census output and the ASGS Edition 3 page gives the approximation caveat and code structure; the usual-residence basis follows the '(ur)' in the custodian's own description, which the glossary distinguishes from place of enumeration.
evidence_quote: An SED is an area legally prescribed for the purpose of returning one or more members to the State or Territory lower houses of parliament.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried only 'State electoral divisions (2021 boundaries) (ur)' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not warn that a Census count by electorate is not a count of electors.

value_domain: ASGS State Electoral Division code (2022 boundaries, usual residence)
value_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, State Electoral Divisions
variable_description: The person's usual address placed on the 2022 state electoral division boundaries, the redistributed counterpart of SEDP on the same 2021 person record. ABS updates the State Electoral Division approximation annually as redistributions occur, and describes the divisions themselves as "an ABS Mesh Block approximation of state electoral districts as defined by state and territory electoral commissions". Holding both vintages lets 2021 Census person counts be reported against either the pre- or post-redistribution map without recoding. It is the person-level twin of SED22D on the dwelling record.
value_definition: A five-digit ASGS code (one digit for state or territory, four for the division) on the 2022 boundary set, with Victoria and Tasmania using a two-part identifier that reflects both lower and upper house regions.
limitation: A person whose SEDP and SEDP22 differ has not moved and has not changed enrolment; only the boundary moved, so the pair cannot be used as any kind of change measure. The approximation also means the column cannot establish an individual's actual electoral district, which only the state electoral commission's roll can do.
rationale: The ASGS Edition 3 page defines the structure, gives the code format and documents the annual boundary updates including 2022. That the '22' suffix denotes the boundary vintage follows from the custodian's own description, '2022 boundaries'.
evidence_quote: State Electoral Divisions are an ABS Mesh Block approximation of state electoral districts as defined by state and territory electoral commissions.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'State electoral divisions (2022 boundaries) (ur)' with the generic no-value-list sentence as definition and limitation, so it did not explain the second boundary vintage or its relation to SEDP.

value_domain: Census sex category
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2021, Sex (SEXP)
variable_description: The person's sex as reported on the Census form, published as male or female. ABS defines the variable as recording "each person's sex", and states that "a person's sex is based on their sex characteristics, such as their chromosomes, hormones and reproductive organs". A non-binary sex response option was added to the 2021 form, but the output categories stayed at male and female. Sex is imputed when it is missing, and SXFP on the 2011 person record flags an imputed value.
value_definition: Two output categories, 1 male and 2 female, and no supplementary codes: sex is imputed where the question is not answered. The non-binary input option added in 2021 is not carried through to output.
limitation: It is not gender identity. ABS notes that respondents were confused about the difference, so some transgender and gender diverse people answered on identity rather than sex characteristics, and a non-binary response that came with no male or female answer is allocated to male or female at random. Non-response was 4.7 per cent in 2021 and 5.8 per cent in 2016, and that gap is closed by imputation rather than by a reported answer.
rationale: The Census Dictionary page defines the mnemonic in the ABS's own words, states the output categories, records the 2021 addition of a non-binary input option and publishes the non-response rates.
evidence_quote: This variable records each person's sex. A person's sex is based on their sex characteristics, such as their chromosomes, hormones and reproductive organs.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the one-word description 'Sex' with the generic no-value-list sentence printed twice, so it did not distinguish sex from gender, note the imputation, or give the non-response rate.

value_domain: Census status in employment category
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2021, Status in employment (SIEMP)
variable_description: Whether the person worked as an employee, as the owner manager of their own business, or as a contributing family worker, in the main job they held in the week before Census night. ABS defines it as a variable that "defines a person's employment status for the main job held in the week prior to Census Night". The owner manager categories split on whether the business is incorporated and on whether it has employees, which is how the Census separates a company director from a sole trader. It is derived from several answers together — whether the person had a job, whether they worked for an employer or their own business, the legal structure of the business and its employee count.
value_definition: Eleven categories: employee; owner manager of an incorporated enterprise with employees, without employees or employees not stated; the same three for unincorporated enterprises; contributing family worker; plus not stated, not applicable and overseas visitor.
limitation: It covers the main job only, so a person who is an employee by day and runs a business at night appears as one or the other and second jobs are invisible. The not applicable code is not a residual category of workers: it pools people aged under 15, the unemployed, people not in the labour force and those whose labour force status was not stated, so it must not be treated as 'no employment status'.
rationale: The Census Dictionary page defines the mnemonic, lists the eleven categories, describes the questions the variable is derived from and states exactly what the not applicable code comprises.
evidence_quote: This variable defines a person's employment status for the main job held in the week prior to Census Night.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Status in Employment' with the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation, so it did not say the reference is the main job in one week or what falls into not applicable.

value_domain: Sex of lone parent
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2021, Sex of lone parent (SLPP)
variable_description: Flags a person as a lone parent and gives their sex, so one-parent families can be split into mother-headed and father-headed. ABS defines it as indicating "the sex, either male or female, of lone parents present in the household on Census Night". Only people coded as lone parents in RLHP carry a value; partners, children, dependent students, other relatives and non-family members are all not applicable. It is the person-level companion to the one-parent family categories in the family record's FMCF.
value_definition: Two substantive codes, 1 male lone parent and 2 female lone parent, plus @ for not applicable and V for overseas visitor.
limitation: 'Lone' means no coresident partner, not sole care: a parent whose children spend part of their time at another address is coded as if this household were the whole picture, and shared-care arrangements are invisible in the Census. The not applicable code covers everyone who is not a lone parent, including all partnered parents, so this column cannot be used as a denominator of parents.
rationale: The Census Dictionary page defines the mnemonic in ABS's own words, gives the four codes and lists in detail who falls into not applicable.
evidence_quote: This variable indicates the sex, either male or female, of lone parents present in the household on Census Night.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried only 'Sex of Lone Parent' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not say that only lone parents carry a value or warn that lone does not mean sole care.

value_domain: ASGS Section of State code
value_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, Section of State
variable_description: Whether the dwelling sits in a major urban centre, another urban centre, a bounded locality or the rural balance of its state. ABS defines Section of State as grouping "together Urban Centres and Localities (UCLs) into comparable classes based on the population of the UCL according to the 2021 Census", with major urban meaning a centre of 100,000 or more. This is the urban-rural axis, distinct from the access-to-services axis that RAD measures on the same 2021 dwelling record, and UCLD beside it names the actual centre. SOSRD gives a finer cut of the same idea.
value_definition: A two-digit hierarchical code: one digit for state or territory, one for the class — major urban, other urban, bounded locality or rural balance. Special purpose codes are 7 for migratory-offshore-shipping, 9 for no usual address and ZZ for outside Australia.
limitation: The class comes from the population of the whole urban centre, not from density around the dwelling, so a house on the fringe of a city of a million is major urban while an identical house in a town of 90,000 is not. It is also recalculated from each Census's population, so a growing town changes class without anything about the dwelling changing.
rationale: The ASGS Edition 3 Section of State page gives the definition, the four classes with their population thresholds and the two-digit code structure including special purpose codes.
evidence_quote: Section of State (SOS) groups together Urban Centres and Localities (UCLs) into comparable classes based on the population of the UCL according to the 2021 Census of Population and Housing.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Section of state (en)' with the generic no-value-list sentence as definition and limitation, so it did not say that the classes are population thresholds on urban centres or how it differs from remoteness.

value_domain: ASGS Section of State code (usual residence)
value_source: ABS Census geography glossary, Section of State (SOS)
variable_description: Whether the person usually lived in a major urban centre, another urban centre, a bounded locality or the rural balance. ABS defines Section of State as grouping "Urban Centres and Localities (UCLs) into classes of urban areas based on population size, and the remainder is rural", so this is the standard urban-rural split for Census person data. Because it is coded to usual residence it can differ from SOSD on the dwelling the person was counted in. SOSRP on the same 2021 person record gives the finer population bands.
value_definition: A two-digit ASGS code combining state or territory with the class — major urban (100,000 or more), other urban, bounded locality, rural balance — plus special codes for migratory-offshore-shipping, no usual address and outside Australia.
limitation: Urban here means a built-up centre above a population threshold, not a lifestyle or a density, so a small satellite town swallowed by a city can sit in a different class from the suburb next to it. The classification is rebuilt each Census from that Census's counts, so a change in a person's class between Censuses is not proof they moved.
rationale: The Census geography glossary gives the Census-specific Section of State definition and the ASGS Edition 3 page supplies the classes, thresholds and code structure.
evidence_quote: Section of State (SOS) groups Urban Centres and Localities (UCLs) into classes of urban areas based on population size, and the remainder is rural.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried only 'Section of state (ur)' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not say what the classes are or that they are recalculated at each Census.

value_domain: ASGS Section of State Range code
value_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, Section of State Range
variable_description: The population-size band of the urban centre or locality the dwelling sits in, a finer cut of what SOSD reports as four broad classes. ABS defines Section of State Range as grouping "together Urban Centres and Localities (UCLs) into comparable classes based on the population of the UCL according to the 2021 Census", splitting major urban into three bands from a million or more down to 100,000 to 249,999, and other urban into five smaller bands. Where SOSD says only 'other urban', SOSRD says whether the town holds 50,000 people or 1,000. Both sit on the 2021 dwelling record and describe the same place.
value_definition: A three-digit hierarchical code — state or territory, then the Section of State class, then the range identifier — over eleven bands from 1 million or more down to bounded localities of 499 or fewer and the rural balance, with 79 for migratory populations and 99 for no usual address.
limitation: The band describes the urban centre as a whole, not the dwelling's surroundings, so every dwelling in a city of a million shares one code and an inner suburb cannot be told from an outer one. The bands are also recomputed from each Census's population, so a town can move up a band through growth while nothing about the dwelling changes.
rationale: The ASGS Edition 3 Section of State Range page gives the definition, the eleven population bands with their thresholds and the three-digit code structure including the special purpose codes.
evidence_quote: Section of State Range (SOSR) groups together Urban Centres and Localities (UCLs) into comparable classes based on the population of the UCL according to the 2021 Census of Population and Housing.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Section of state range (en)' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it never explained what the ranges are ranges of, or how the column adds to SOSD beside it.

value_domain: ASGS Section of State Range code (usual residence)
value_source: ABS Census geography glossary, Section of State Ranges (SOSR)
variable_description: The population-size band of the urban centre or locality the person usually lived in, on the 2021 person record. ABS notes that Section of State Range "provides a more detailed classification than Section of State (SOS)", cutting the broad urban-rural classes into bands by the population of the centre. It is the column to reach for when town size is the point of the analysis — comparing outcomes in centres of 50,000 against centres of 5,000 — where SOSP would call both 'other urban'. Because it is coded to usual residence it can differ from SOSRD on the dwelling the person was counted in.
value_definition: A three-digit ASGS code combining state or territory, the Section of State class and the range identifier, over eleven bands from 1 million or more down to bounded localities of 499 or fewer, plus the rural balance and special purpose codes.
limitation: It measures the size of the centre a person lives in, not their distance from services, so it cannot substitute for the remoteness classification RANP on the same record: a town of 20,000 can be Inner Regional or Very Remote. Band membership also depends on the current Census's population count, so the same town can be in different bands in 2016 and 2021.
rationale: The Census geography glossary states how Section of State Range relates to Section of State, and the ASGS Edition 3 page supplies the bands, thresholds and code structure.
evidence_quote: Section of State Range (SOSR) provides a more detailed classification than Section of State (SOS).
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried only 'Section of state range (ur)' with the generic no-value-list sentence as definition and limitation, so it did not say what distinguishes it from SOSP or warn against reading it as remoteness.

value_domain: Spouse or partner indicator within a couple family
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2021, Spouse/partner indicator (SPIP)
variable_description: Marks, within a couple family, whether the person is the family reference person or that person's spouse or partner. ABS defines it as recording "the usually resident husband/wife/partner or de facto partner in a couple family". It is how a couple is reconstructed from the 2021 person record: one person in each couple family carries code 1 and one carries code 2, so joining them pairs the partners. It covers registered and de facto partners alike, and includes a partner reported as temporarily absent on Census night.
value_definition: Four codes: 1 family reference person, 2 spouse or partner, @ not applicable and V overseas visitor.
limitation: It does not describe the relationship — whether the couple is registered or de facto, and same-sex or opposite-sex, comes from RLCP and SSCF, not from here. Code 1 is also not a status: the reference person is a coding convention, so it must not be read as the main earner or the household head. A partner who does not usually live in the household is outside the variable entirely.
rationale: The Census Dictionary page defines the mnemonic, gives its four codes, and states that it covers both registered and de facto partners and those reported temporarily absent.
evidence_quote: This variable records the usually resident husband/wife/partner or de facto partner in a couple family.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Spouse/partner indicator' with the generic no-value-list sentence as definition and limitation, so it did not say the column is what pairs two person records into one couple.

value_domain: Location of spouse in a couple family
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2021, Location of spouse (SPLF)
variable_description: For a couple family, whether the second partner was actually there on Census night or was reported as temporarily away. ABS defines it as recording "whether the usually resident husband/wife/partner or de facto partner is present or temporarily absent from a couple family on Census Night". It sits on the family record beside the counts of temporarily absent children (CDCAF, CDSAF, CNDAF), so the family table can be read as who was present against who belongs. A temporarily absent spouse still counts as part of the family, which is why FMCF can show a couple family in which only one adult was enumerated.
value_definition: Three codes: 1 present, 2 temporarily absent and @ not applicable. Not applicable covers one-parent families, other families, non-family and non-classifiable households, unoccupied dwellings and non-private dwellings.
limitation: Temporarily absent is not separation, and the code says neither where the partner was nor for how long, so a fly-in fly-out worker and someone on a fortnight's holiday look identical. The absent partner also has no person record in this dwelling, so their age, income, occupation and education are missing even though the family counts them, and per-family averages built from person records will be biased.
rationale: The Census Dictionary page defines the mnemonic, gives its three codes and lists the family and household types that fall into not applicable.
evidence_quote: This variable records whether the usually resident husband/wife/partner or de facto partner is present or temporarily absent from a couple family on Census Night.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried only 'Location of Spouse' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not say that an absent spouse is still counted in the family or that their person-level attributes are missing.

value_domain: Same-sex couple family indicator
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2021, Same-sex couple indicator (SSCF)
variable_description: Whether the couple at the centre of this family is a male same-sex couple, a female same-sex couple or an opposite-sex couple. ABS defines it as a variable that "uses relationship information to indicate whether a family are a same-sex couple family", and it is derived during processing from the reported relationship and the sex of the two partners rather than asked directly. That is why ABS states it "does not have a non-response rate as it is created during Census processing by using responses from more than one question on the Census form". It is the family-record summary of what RLCP records for each partner on the person record.
value_definition: Four codes: 1 male same-sex couple, 2 female same-sex couple, 3 opposite-sex couple and @ not applicable. Not applicable covers one-parent families, other families, lone person and group households, non-classifiable households, unoccupied and non-private dwellings and migratory areas.
limitation: Having no non-response rate does not make the count complete: the derivation always produces a value, so an error in either input — a couple who described themselves as flatmates, or a misreported sex — becomes a confident wrong answer rather than a missing one. The column also describes the couple a person lives in, not anyone's sexual orientation, and ABS warns that the definition of a family differs between statistical collections, so care is needed comparing these counts with other family data.
rationale: The Census Dictionary page defines the mnemonic, lists its four codes and its not applicable scope, and publishes both the no-non-response-rate note and the warning about comparing family definitions across collections.
evidence_quote: this variable does not have a non-response rate as it is created during Census processing by using responses from more than one question on the Census form
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Same Sex Couple Indicator' with the generic no-value-list sentence as definition and limitation, so it did not say the variable is derived rather than reported, or explain why the absence of a non-response rate is not a sign of quality.

value_domain: ASGS state and territory code (usual residence one year ago)
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2021, Place of usual residence one year ago (PUR1P)
variable_description: The state or territory the person usually lived in one year before the Census, the coarsest cut of the one-year-ago address question. ABS defines the source variable as recording "the geographic area in which a person usually lived one year before the Census", output from SA2 upward, so this column is that answer aggregated to state. Read against STEUCP on the same row it gives an interstate migration flow over twelve months, while SA2U1P gives the finer version of the same move. Children under one year old are not applicable, and someone who lived overseas a year earlier gets an overseas code rather than a state.
value_definition: A one-digit ASGS state and territory code, with additional categories for other territories, migratory-offshore-shipping, no usual address, overseas and not stated.
limitation: It cannot see a move within a state, which is the great majority of moves, so an unchanged value is not evidence that the person stayed put. The overseas category has no country attached, so it marks an arrival without saying from where and does not separate a returning Australian from a new migrant. Non-response on the one-year-ago question was 6.0 per cent in 2021 and 8.6 per cent in 2016.
rationale: The Census Dictionary page for the one-year-ago question defines what the address refers to, names the geographic levels it is output at including state and territory, lists the special categories and gives the non-response rates.
evidence_quote: This variable records the geographic area in which a person usually lived one year before the Census.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried only 'State/territory of usual address 1 year ago' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not say that intrastate moves are invisible or that overseas is a single undifferentiated code.

value_domain: ASGS state and territory of usual residence five years earlier
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2021, Place of usual residence five years ago (PUR5P)
variable_description: The state or territory a person usually lived in five years before the Census, held on the person table for 2011, 2016 and 2021. It is the state-level roll-up of the underlying place-of-usual-residence variable, which the Census Dictionary defines as recording "the geographic area in which a person usually lived five years before the Census" and codes to SA2 before aggregating upward. Read it against STEUCP, the state of current usual residence, to get the standard interstate migration measure, and against UAI5P, which says whether the person was at the same address, elsewhere in Australia or overseas. It applies to people aged five years and over, so anyone born since the previous Census is not applicable.
value_definition: A single state or territory code from the ASGS main structure in force for that Census, with separate categories for overseas five years earlier, not stated, not applicable and overseas visitor. Where the SA2 could not be determined the response falls to a state-not-further-defined category.
limitation: It cannot see a move inside a state. Someone who moved from Cairns to Melbourne and someone who moved across a single Melbourne suburb both changed address, but only the first changes this value, so it understates mobility badly in the large states. It also holds one point five years back, not a history, so a move away and back within the window is invisible.
rationale: STEU5P is the state-level output of the Census place-of-usual-residence-five-years-ago concept, and the 2021 Census Dictionary page for PUR5P gives that concept's definition, its SA2 base, its aggregation to state and territory, and its five-years-and-over scope.
evidence_quote: This variable records the geographic area in which a person usually lived five years before the Census.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried only the custodian's wording, 'State/territory of usual address 5 years ago', with the generic 'does not publish a finite value list' sentence as both the value definition and the limitation, so it never said this is usual residence rather than where the person was counted, nor that it is derived from an SA2-coded address.

value_domain: ASGS state and territory of enumeration for the dwelling
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2021 glossary, Place of enumeration
variable_description: The state or territory the dwelling record was enumerated in, and the coarsest of the dwelling table's geography columns. It sits with SA1UCD, SA2UCD, SA3UCD and SA4UCD, described in the 2011 and 2016 metadata as the SA1 to SA4 'of dwelling address', and in 2021 with MBUCD, GCCSAD, SUAD, UCLD and TRD, all carrying the '(en)' tag for place of enumeration, which the Census glossary defines as "the place at which the person is counted on Census Night, which may not be where they usually live". Because a dwelling does not move, its enumeration state and the state it stands in are the same thing; the distinction only bites on the person table, where STEUCP is usual residence instead.
value_definition: A single ASGS state and territory code, the top level of the hierarchy that runs Mesh Block to SA1 to SA2 to SA3 to SA4 to state and territory, together with the Other Territories category and the migratory, off-shore and shipping category.
limitation: It is not where the household usually lives. A holiday house occupied on Census Night by a Victorian family is a New South Wales record here, so any count built on this column is a de facto count: the ABS reports East Pilbara with 39,529 people enumerated against 25,443 usual residents, and Rockingham with 131,213 enumerated against 135,678 usual residents.
